analysis.one_liner: Requires AI robocalls to disclose they are AI and doubles penalties for AI voice-impersonation fraud.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan QUIET Act, with 27 cosponsors from both parties, has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee since February 2025 with no hearing, vote, or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The QUIET Act would amend the telephone consumer protection law to require that any robocall or robotext using artificial intelligence to sound like a person say so at the start of the message. It would also double the maximum fines and forfeitures for callers who use AI to impersonate a real person or company to defraud someone, and it applies to violations after the bill becomes law.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone with a phone, especially older adults and other frequent targets of AI voice-clone scams that impersonate family members, government agencies, or companies to trick people out of money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Phone users targeted by AI scam calls

how_it_helps.text: Any robocall or robotext that uses AI to emulate a human must state at the beginning that AI is being used, so recipients know they are listening to a machine [S2][S3].

When a caller uses AI to impersonate a person or entity with intent to defraud, cause harm, or wrongfully obtain something of value, the maximum forfeiture penalty and the maximum criminal fine are doubled [S2][S3].

The bill broadens the legal definition of robocalls to cover artificially generated voices and messages, including SMS, MMS, and RCS texts, closing a gap as scam technology moves beyond traditional auto-dialers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Robocall operators and AI-impersonation scammers, who would face a new disclosure requirement and doubled fines; honest telemarketers would bear modest compliance costs to add an AI disclosure at the start of calls.

drawbacks.text: A disclosure at the start of a call is a modest remedy: a scammer already breaking the law by impersonating someone is unlikely to pause and announce that AI is being used, so the main practical effect on fraud comes from doubled penalties, which still depend on enforcement and catch rates [S3].
The bill doubles maximum penalties but leaves underlying enforcement unchanged, so its real-world impact depends on regulators pursuing AI-impersonation cases under the higher caps [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are small and fall on the telemarketing and AI-call industries, while the benefit is real but incremental: clearer labeling of AI calls and steeper penalties for impersonation fraud. It is a targeted consumer-protection update rather than a sweeping fix for robocall scams, and it leaves the hard problem of catching anonymous overseas scammers largely untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has remained ever since with no hearing or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Eric Sorensen (D-IL), joined by Rep. Juan Ciscomani (R-AZ), introduced the QUIET Act on February 5, 2025 [S1][S3].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which is the committee that would consider it first [S5].
It has gathered 27 cosponsors from both parties — 22 of 217 House Democrats and 5 of 223 House Republicans [S4].
Since the referral on February 5, 2025, the only recorded action is the sponsor's introductory remarks on February 6, 2025; no markup, hearing, or floor vote has occurred [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Robocall operators and AI-impersonation scammers benefit from continued inaction; no one gains from the bill itself yet, because it has not passed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Robocall operators and AI scam callers

for.name: Rep. Eric Sorensen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the QUIET Act and gave introductory remarks on the House floor the next day.

for.name: Rep. Juan Ciscomani
for.what_they_did: Joined Sorensen as the bill's Republican original cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor is a Democrat and the original cosponsor a Republican; the 27 cosponsors include 22 House Democrats and 5 House Republicans, and no recorded opposition appears in the action history.

industries.note: The bill requires a disclosure whenever AI is used to emulate a human and doubles the maximum fines for AI impersonation used to defraud, raising compliance costs and legal exposure for the call industry. Those costs fall on operators that profit by reaching phone users with automated messages without their knowledge of what they are hearing.

Vendors selling AI voice and text tools to legitimate call operations would face a new disclosure duty on their customers' behalf, while the same technology used to impersonate people for fraud carries doubled penalties. Legitimate business demand for AI calling tools continues either way.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action in the months since its February 2025 referral, the bill follows the typical path for a first-term backbench consumer-protection bill: it will likely remain in the Energy and Commerce Committee unless its sponsors push for a hearing or attach it to a larger telecommunications package. Its bipartisan sponsorship gives it a path if leadership chooses to act, but most referred bills never reach the floor.
